blocks.x: The show is called Speaking of Blues. And tonight we have a special guest on the show. A lady whose name is Mary.
Little Brother recorded a song and it was I think in 1952. It had something to do with the Victory Club.

This was one Sunday morning boy. And old Papa Ammons was over there, Abbot, before he passed. Boy you talking about some fun we had. He and Papa Yassid, they double headed the piano boy. And we danced there that morning till 9, 10 o'clock. That reminds me of Bigfoot Clows at the Victory Club. You ever heard Bigfoot Clows play? He and Sweet Frank Williams. Along about 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning, Milt Moore and Jack Teagarden came by. I run into a little girl with a green dress on and some red stocket. Boy that little chick was gone. She was a solid Senator. I run into a little girl with a green dress on and some red stocking for her. Boy, that little chick was gone. She was a solid sender. Boy, she really couldn't boogie.

A classic by Little Brother Montgomery, to say the least. And I'd like to remind you, this is WLDC at Loyola University, and we're in New Orleans. And we're doing an interview with Mrs. Lee Collins, whose husband is Trumpeter Lee Collins. And she has written a book, and it's entitled, Oh, Didn't He Ramble? And we're trying to talk about Lee and something about the book and get into a few things about it. What inspired you to write a book about your husband? Well, Lee.
He did it himself. Lee wanted it written. He wanted it written. He told me to take down everything he would tell me. Sometimes he would write it on himself, longhand. And I would type it up.
Just memories he had of...

All his memories. It's strictly about him. And so I did. Of course, through the years, a little before he passed, the last chapter that was written, I knew I was a part of it. So I could easily finish it up. Yeah. But he, he insists, even though he was ill, to keep the manuscripts and be sure that I find someone that would put it in, you know... In print. In print. Right. So I did. And I tried several places. You know how that is. You go along and you send it to a publisher. This publisher will keep it a while, and he sent it back, rejected. I was once, one publisher kept it so long, I thought, sure, I was going to get it published. But it didn't happen. But finally I found a publisher. And so happened. So this is the book. Oh, didn't he ramble?
Is it just memories of Lee's life or is it... Do you have any interpretation of what his contribution was by friends?

Well, it's about a lot of his friends also. You know, he writes about all the great carnet players. He named them in his book. Mm-hmm. And trombone players. In fact, all the musicians that played in New Orleans, as far back he can remember, he named them in his book. Mm-hmm. Gave them a lot of credit. He didn't put any bouquets on his own shoulder, but he did for the other musicians. Yeah. And I don't think you will find any book written about jazz that really contributed a great deal to the other musicians like Lee did. Yeah. And he felt that he was very happy, you know, to do this. And he wanted this book printed so he could, as he said, contribute to some of those that have forgotten. Because a lot of musicians don't mention some of the musicians he tells about in his book. Yeah. Yeah. But they were here. Right. And he felt that they should be heard about. And that's why the book is out.
Mm-hmm.
Oh, didn't he ramble? Yeah. Why that title?
Why that title? Why that title?
Well, that title is what they play for musicians coming back from the cemetery. From the cemetery.
Right.
Funnels.
Yeah.
And, but, oh, didn't he ramble doesn't mean, but it meant that he was the one that did a lot of rambling around. Yeah. And so that's why he put the title, oh, didn't he ramble? Yeah.
That, well, I know it, it, uh, I was thinking in, in terms of him, him, see himself being a rambler, but you took it from, from a song.
From a song. But he, but part of that, just what you were thinking too. Yeah.
He was, he moved a lot.

We combined the, they're both things together. Yeah. See, uh, because he, when he was a young man, you know, wild, a little, on the wild side a little bit when he was young. Yeah. So, he, he tells all of that in the book. And so I think that's what he had in mind when he said, uh, have the title, didn't he ramble?
Did you, uh, add anything after he died or, or?

Uh, yes, I did. A lot of, uh, of a life together. Yeah. Interpretation. Yeah, your interpretation. When we first met and, uh, traveling and a few little things, uh, not too much about myself, but a little bit. And so that's how I finished up with it. So, uh, uh. Because it was a lot more could have been told, but he was too ill. He, you know, he was very ill for, for quite a long time. For two years, really, emphysema just worked on you like that. You last so long and then that's it. Yeah. There's no cure for it.
Mm-hmm.
And that's the sad part about it. That's a lot of times that he, uh, said he often wished that he'd had, uh, tuberculosis because you could cure that, but you can't cure emphysema.
Mm-hmm.

And two or three times he was very despondent, you know. Sometimes he didn't want to see his friends. They would come to visit him. And, uh, Mr. Robichaud came to see. Joe Robichaud? Right. Joe. Oh, he admired him, but Mr. Robichaud never took him in the band because he said Lee was a little too wild. And Lee, but Lee really. I'm surprised Joe Robichaud said. Well, at that time, when he was young, he played a different style of music. I'm sorry.
So that's why.

Yeah. But, uh, when Lee was ill, he came to see him. Yeah. He was in Chicago to visit his, uh, his son. And so he did, and you know, um, other Joe Robichaud, he, uh, recorded with Lee, with this Astoristrut.
Right.
That was made. And Sidney Ayrton, Ayrton, Ayrton, he's, uh, a great friend, a clarinet player. And he got him to record with him.
Would Lee consider himself a successful musician? And, and, and in what sense would he?

Well, he knew he could play. But he never did, one thing he never mentioned about being successful musician. But he knew that he could play, he could walk out. One thing that I noticed, that I knew that he could do, he could walk out on there, on a stage or a bandstand and play and you would never catch him missing a note. He knew a way of, of, uh, going out. He never, in other words, he never had a bad night.
No.
He never said that. Even when he was ill, very ill, he never did.
Mm-hmm.
And the last, and the first time that I ever knew that he missed a note that was in Paris on the stage. And I knew he was very ill that night.
You could, I mean, well, you could tell, I would suspect.

I, because I was always backstage with him. Yes. And very seldom, he wouldn't, he wouldn't let me, he wouldn't let me leave him. If he had to go, if I stayed home at the hotel where we were, he'd say, well, why can't you go with me tonight? Like that. But this particular night, I did. There were, and he missed it and I looked at him and I begged for him to come off. Mm-hmm. And that was it and he went to the hospital.
I mean, uh, was he ever, uh, despondent or, uh, depressed about, uh, the amount of money he made? Did he say he didn't make a lot? No. Did he make success and money, uh, together?
No. For him? He never, he never, as I said, the money angle, it never bothered him.
As long as he was making ends meet and, uh. That's true.
And support.
What would you, would you say he would have thought he was a successful musician?
No, he liked to make the money, but not to use it for himself. As long as it, uh, he brought it, he brought his money home.
What I'm saying, did he gauge success by his own personal musical?

He did. He did it. He gained it by his own. Mm-hmm. That's the only way he would ever gotten it because he was a tremendous trumpet player. Tremendous. He had a volume, but he never had to use a mic. Oh, yeah. He'd blow you away if you stood in front of him. And it takes, uh, his friend, uh, I was talking to the other night, Mr. Joe Merez, and he was saying about Lee, he said, my goodness, see that guy stand up. You better get the mic away. You better get the mic away. And that's just the way he blew. Yeah. Terrific. Mm-hmm. And I admired, well, I did admire, he was my husband still and all, but I admired him. Right. Great deal. Because I would be happy if I could see him up there blowing, he's happy. When he was happy, he would blow, he would look down on me and do little funny things, you know, meddle with me up on the stage. Right. And that's the way we live.
So your, your, your, your fondest memories are your days with Lee. Right. Those last. Still missing. Yeah.
Really. Yeah. My happy days.
There were, there were other musicians that Lee worked with. Uh, one was, uh, Sidney Benet.
Sidney Bichet.
Sidney Bichet.
Right. I'm sorry. Uh-huh. Sidney Bichet, well, he was our great friend. Also, I have, I will show you, I have a photograph of Lee and Sidney.

Lee and Sidney together? I have it. Yeah. Yeah. Sometimes I wish this was television and we could show, hold up photographs and show photographs, but we can't. That's true. But we don't have, we couldn't get recordings of Lee tonight for some reason. We don't have any. And, uh, we've been playing music by his friends. So, uh, you know, just bear with us. And here's a recording by Sidney Bichet. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. ¶¶

¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ Sidney Bechet and a recording called The KC Man Blues. I'm not sure. That was from, I think, 19 and late 40s. It was a live recording. I'm trying to get the date on that. Let me see. July 14, 1947. A fine recording by Sidney Bechet. Our guest tonight is Lee Collins. Mrs. Lee Collins, I'm sorry. We're still talking about a book which she wrote called... Oh, Didn't He Ramble? Didn't He Ramble? Oh, Didn't He Ramble? I was getting a feedback in my headphones. I'm still getting another one. I have to turn these down. Lee's last days were not happy days or... No. ...reflection on his life, time with friends, or...

Well, he really, when he was in the hospitals and things, he was very unhappy because he always had hopes of blowing his trumpet again. He was despondent to what extent, once, that he took about 20 Nevitol. And we went to the hospital. I got back home in time to get him in the hospital. And he really, he always said he didn't want to live if he couldn't blow. But I always tried to encourage him and tell him that he would blow again. And that's what his doctors insist on me doing. Because his... He needed some hope to... Right. He had to have it. And one incident that happened to him, and to this day, I mention it every time I get an opportunity to do so. Chicago have a system there that people that attempt suicide or they think they are something, they have a habit of sending them to a state institution for, you know, psych treatments. Well, he was sent out there to be friends. A judge determines what's to be done. Right. So, a friend of his and I were out there that day and we carried his clothes thinking we were bringing back home. And this judge said, no, he couldn't be brought back. He'd have to go and take these treatments. Well, he was very ill at the time. He'd had pneumonia also. Mm-hmm. So, they did send him out there. Well, I used to go see him and he said, oh, when he first sent him out there, they put drunks and whatnot mixed up with patients that shouldn't be. Yeah. And as soon as he got in, they told him to mop or do something, but anyway, they beat him up. And when I got out and found out he was beating up, I insisted they put him in the hospital after I got out there. So, they would not release him to me. I had to get a lawyer. So, I got a lawyer and this lawyer looked like to me he was not going to get him out there. I went to the superintendent, but not released him. So, I decided on doing this. He could walk on the grounds. I said, look, they're not letting you out of here and you've got to have treatment. Come on, let's go. But we both, I was so frightened because you know you're not supposed to do that. Yeah. Thank you. So, I walked him out the gate. You saw? And we took buses and streetcars every direction because I didn't want them because they would have probably, you know, arrested me for taking him. And I took him home. Then I took him to the hospital. And so, I called up the superintendent and told him that I had him in the hospital. And so, he said, well, come out and we want to straighten this out. And they got frightened after that. Yeah. So, they wanted me to come out and sign the papers that, you know, they released him. But I refused to do it. So, then they wrote me letters and letters to come. But I still would not go. And that was when Lee stayed in the hospital for quite a long time. Well, the jazz club and the musicians decided, well, the money was going then, whatever money
we were spending. Whatever money you had.
What we had was really gone. So, they decided to give her a benefit.
Who played, who showed for the benefit?

Oh, my goodness. I'm going to get to that. But the benefit was supposed to be given at the Blue Note. Louis Armstrong and Gary Crosby were there in Chicago, Chicago Theater. And something, some reason, I don't know who did it, but they canceled it. So, the musician decided not to give it in Chicago, decided to give it out in the suburbs. They did. So, the Dukes of Dixieland came. And musicians from England, oh, several bands came. And they played for this benefit, which was quite successful. You couldn't get in the hall. And that's how that benefit ended up. But Lee never got well after this episode. He was in and out of the hospital quite often. And so, he was still discouraged. And then I had to watch him when he got home because the doctor said he may, you know, attempt it again. But he didn't. He just gave up and he refused to see his friends. And they had the Barno's from Belgium came to see him. And he liked them very much when we were in Europe. And he would not let me put the light on to see, you know, he was wasting away. And so, but on the last go-round, just three days before his death, he asked me to take him out of the hospital. And I did. I brought him home. And he was very happy. But that was it, you know.
Then he died. Right. Right then.
That's the way it happened.
When, after, at his funeral, who was, everybody came?

Well, not exactly because I, really I was tired. And I had, I made the arrangements for the funeral. And it was in our way. In a hurry, in a hurry, in a hurry. Right. And a lot of people said I shouldn't. But nobody realized that with me alone and having everything to do and in and out every night to the hospital, I would sit up. The doctors really insisted I would leave because they figured that I would be in the next bed. But I just couldn't, I couldn't do it. I wanted to be there with him. So, I, then after he passed, I said, well, why not just go ahead and have the funeral? But we had quite a few, you know, musicians and friends there. But it wasn't like it would have been a big funeral. I didn't want that. I was tired.
Yeah, that big funeral. Did, what, what, to sort of sum this up, what, what do you think Lee gave to the music, to the music that he played?

Inspiration. Inspiration. That's what I feel. Inspiration. Happiness. He was always happy, smiling, had a big smile on his face. Young musicians, he would try to tell them right from wrong and what a hard life it was. But if you were a musician and you wanted to play.
It was there.

It was there and you tried and go ahead and do it. And it could be. And he think that music keep youngsters out of mischief. Really. He did? He always said music would. I mean, if they wanted to do it.
Right.

They didn't have to have the inspiration to do it. But he felt that that's the best medicine for youngsters is music. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he was a kid. And he could have been into trouble too. But he didn't. So that's how he felt about it.

So that's what Lee Collins was all about. The book is called, Oh, Didn't He Ramble? I'm still trying to get that. We've been talking for almost 45 minutes. Ms. Collins, I want to thank you for coming by and talking about the book. What publisher is it with?
University of Illinois.
University of Illinois Publishers. Right.
That's true.

And the story of Lee Collins. And just to end it off, another friend of Lee Collins, who he played with for a number of years, Sweet Williams.
